concepts.name: Origins and Historical Context of the Bengal School
key_dimensions: Reaction against the dominance of Company School and Western academic realism introduced under British rule
Role of the Swadeshi Movement and Indian nationalism in shaping an indigenous artistic identity
Distinction between Bengal School as an art movement vs. a nationalist cultural assertion
Overlap with the broader Indian Renaissance and its intellectual currents (Brahmo Samaj, Tagore family)

concepts.name: Abanindranath Tagore: Founder and Ideology
key_dimensions: Nephew of Rabindranath Tagore; role as the principal founder and ideologue of the Bengal School
Rejection of oil painting and Western techniques in favor of wash technique and Eastern aesthetics
Creation of 'Bharat Mata' (1905) as a seminal nationalist artwork — symbolism and context
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Abanindranath's contributions from those of Rabindranath Tagore in visual arts

concepts.name: E.B. Havell's Role and the Calcutta School of Art Controversy
key_dimensions: Ernest Binfield Havell as Principal of Government School of Art, Calcutta — his advocacy for Indian classical art
Controversy over replacing European plaster casts with Mughal miniatures in the school curriculum
Collaborative relationship between Havell and Abanindranath Tagore in reforming art education
UPSC trap: Havell was British, yet a champion of Indian art — distinguishing his role from colonial art imposition

concepts.name: The 'Indian Wash Technique' — Stylistic Hallmark of Bengal School
key_dimensions: Technical description: use of thin, translucent washes of watercolor or ink on paper/silk
Influence drawn from Japanese wash painting (Nihonga technique) and Mughal miniature traditions
Contrast with European oil painting technique — why Bengal School deliberately avoided it
Examples: Abanindranath's 'Arabian Nights' series and 'Passing of Shah Jahan'

concepts.name: Japanese Influence and the 'Indo-Japanese' Style
key_dimensions: Visit of Japanese artists Yokoyama Taikan and Hijkata Hirosuke to Calcutta (1902) — exchange of ideas
Pan-Asian vision: Okakura Kakuzo's 'Asia is One' philosophy and its artistic manifestation
Specific stylistic borrowings: sfumato-like outlines, flat planes of color, lyrical treatment of nature
UPSC trap: Bengal School drew from Japan but is NOT the same as Japanese art — it is a synthesis

concepts.name: Iconographic Sources: Ajanta, Mughal, and Rajput Influences
key_dimensions: Revival of Ajanta fresco techniques and iconographic motifs — spirituality and sensuousness
Selective incorporation of Mughal miniature's delicate line work and compositional balance
Rajput painting's lyrical devotional themes (Krishna, Radha) as subject matter
UPSC trap: Bengal School 'revived' these traditions but did NOT produce classical Indian art — it was a modern synthesis

concepts.name: Nandalal Bose: Second-Generation Leader and Institutional Role
key_dimensions: Student of Abanindranath; considered the greatest muralist and teacher of the Bengal School
Principal of Kala Bhavana, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan — role in institutionalizing the movement
Illustration of the Constitution of India (original hand-illustrated manuscript) — a direct UPSC link
Haripura Posters (1938) for INC session — art used as political/nationalist communication

concepts.name: Kala Bhavana, Santiniketan as an Institutional Hub
key_dimensions: Founded by Rabindranath Tagore in 1919 as the art faculty of Visva-Bharati University
Distinction: Santiniketan was associated with Bengal School but had its own 'Santiniketan School' that went beyond it
Nandalal Bose's role in shaping its curriculum emphasizing craft, nature study, and Indian classical traditions
UPSC trap: Visva-Bharati is a Central University; Kala Bhavana is its art school — not an independent institution

concepts.name: Rabindranath Tagore as Visual Artist — Relationship with Bengal School
key_dimensions: Rabindranath began painting late in life (~1928) with a distinctly different, expressionist style
His art is NOT considered Bengal School — it is more surrealist/expressionist in character
UPSC trap: Rabindranath's nephew Abanindranath founded Bengal School; Rabindranath himself is a separate chapter in Indian art
His doodles ('Kadambari' series) evolved into full canvases — psychological and subconscious themes

concepts.name: Gaganendranath Tagore: Cubism and Caricature
key_dimensions: Elder brother of Abanindranath; associated with Bengal School but pioneered Indian Cubism
First Indian artist to experiment with Cubist techniques — use of faceted planes and artificial lighting
Famous for socio-political caricatures satirizing colonial society and Hindu orthodoxy
UPSC trap: Gaganendranath is associated with Bengal School context but stylistically departed from it — a key distinction

concepts.name: Feminist and Nationalist Symbolism in Bengal School Paintings
key_dimensions: 'Bharat Mata' by Abanindranath (1905) — four-armed goddess holding book, paddy, white cloth, garland as nationalist symbol
Contrast with later Bharat Mata imagery (map-based iconography) — Bengal School's version predates it
Use of feminine divine imagery as a vehicle for anti-colonial sentiment
Role in the Swadeshi movement — art as propaganda and cultural resistance

concepts.name: The 'Passing of Shah Jahan' — Close Reading as UPSC Model
key_dimensions: Painted by Abanindranath Tagore — depicts aging Mughal emperor gazing at Taj Mahal from Agra Fort
Exemplifies wash technique, muted palette, lyrical melancholy — key stylistic features
Nationalist symbolism: mourning of a glorious Indian (Mughal) past under colonial subjugation
Frequently cited as the defining masterpiece of the Bengal School — used for identification in Prelims

concepts.name: Criticism and Decline of the Bengal School
key_dimensions: Criticism by modernists (e.g., Progressive Artists' Group) as being too sentimental and backward-looking
F.N. Souza and the Progressive Artists' Group (1947) as a direct counter-movement
Internal critique: the style became formulaic and commercially imitative by the 1930s–40s
Paradox: a 'nationalist' school that drew heavily from Japanese and foreign influences

concepts.name: Bengal School vs. Company School — Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Company School (Patna/Murshidabad): hybrid Indo-European naturalism for British patrons — watercolor on Western paper
Bengal School: deliberate anti-Western, revivalist aesthetic for nationalist patrons
Geographical and patronage overlap in Bengal — yet ideologically opposed
UPSC trap: Both used watercolor but for entirely different purposes and with different aesthetics

concepts.name: Bengal School vs. Progressive Artists' Group — Ideological Contrast
key_dimensions: Progressive Artists' Group (PAG, 1947, Bombay): F.N. Souza, S.H. Raza, M.F. Husain, K.H. Ara, S.K. Bakre, H.A. Gade
PAG embraced Western modernism (Cubism, Expressionism, abstraction) — opposite of Bengal School's revivalism
Bengal School as pre-Independence nationalist art; PAG as post-Independence cosmopolitan art
UPSC trap: MF Husain painted Hindu goddesses but was NOT Bengal School — he was PAG

concepts.name: Asit Kumar Haldar and Surendranath Ganguly — Lesser-Known Practitioners
key_dimensions: Asit Kumar Haldar: student of Abanindranath; worked on murals at Ajanta-inspired settings; taught at Kala Bhavana
Surendranath Ganguly: known for portraiture within Bengal School idiom — often confused with calendar art
Both demonstrate the stylistic range within Bengal School beyond its iconic masters
UPSC angle: questions sometimes name lesser artists to test depth of knowledge

concepts.name: Okakura Kakuzo and Pan-Asian Aesthetics
key_dimensions: Japanese philosopher-critic who visited Calcutta (1902) and inspired the Indo-Japanese artistic exchange
His book 'The Ideals of the East' (1903) articulated 'Asia is One' — foundational text for Pan-Asian art philosophy
Influence on Abanindranath's conceptualization of a unified 'Eastern' aesthetic against Western dominance
UPSC trap: Okakura was Japanese, not Indian — but his philosophy was foundational for the Bengal School

concepts.name: Bengal School's Treatment of Mythology and Spirituality
key_dimensions: Predominance of Hindu mythological themes — Krishna, Durga, scenes from Mahabharata and Ramayana
Buddhist themes drawn from Ajanta — compassionate Bodhisattvas, Jataka tales
Sufi and Islamic themes also present (e.g., Abanindranath's Arabian Nights series) — the movement was NOT exclusively Hindu
UPSC trap: Bengal School is often stereotyped as Hindu revivalist, but it had a pluralist iconographic vocabulary

concepts.name: Legacy and Influence on Indian Art Education
key_dimensions: Bengal School institutionalized the idea of a distinctly 'Indian' fine art pedagogy — influence on art school curricula nationwide
Nandalal Bose's Santiniketan model influenced craft-based, nature-integrated art education
The original hand-illustrated Constitution of India (1950) as the most tangible political legacy
Paradox of legacy: the very movement that resisted Western art became the new 'academic' orthodoxy that later modernists rebelled against
